extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, applicants, and practitioners evaluating US patent subject-matter eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing U.S. patent claims under the 2019 USPTO Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG), including Step 2A (two-prong) and Step 2B analyses and illustrative examples (Examples 37–46). Intended to help determine whether claims recite judicial exceptions and whether additional elements integrate those exceptions into a practical application or provide an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of Abstract Ideas (three categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas are categorized into three enumerated groupings: (1) mathematical concepts — relationships, formulas, calculations; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity — fundamental economic practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing personal behavior; (3) mental processes — observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that don't fall into one of these groupings should not typically be treated as reciting an abstract idea. Use these groupings to determine whether a claim recites a judicial exception under Step 2A Prong One.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea identified by the three groupings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim does not recite a judicial exception under Prong One, the claim is eligible and no further Step 2A/2B analysis is needed. Use the abstract-idea groupings to assess whether subject matter is an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a judicial exception, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the answer to Prong Two is YES (the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application), the claim is eligible and Step 2B is not required. Practical-application analysis is broader than an 'inventive concept' analysis and focuses on whether additional elements meaningfully apply the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of how a claim may integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include: improvement to functioning of a computer or other technology; applied/used in conjunction with a particular machine; effecting a transformation of an article to a different state or thing; applies the judicial exception in some other meaningful way; beyond merely linking the use to a technological environment. These factors support a finding that Prong Two is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Mere instructions to apply" indicators (NOT practical application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claim elements/limitations that do not show integration into a practical application and thus are NOT sufficient under Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include: adding the words 'apply it' with the judicial exception; mere instructions to apply on a generic computer; field-of-use limitations; generic linking to a technological environment; adding insignificant extra-solution activity. Presence of these tends to weigh against finding a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Additional elements / inventive concept analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If Prong Two does not show integration into a practical application (i.e., claim is directed to an abstract idea), analyze whether additional elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for elements that go BEYOND well-understood, routine, conventional activities. Berkheimer factors apply (i.e., courts may treat some aspects as factual questions). Generic computer components are not enough. The 'inventive concept' must be more than just the abstract idea itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of specification and case-by-case factual record
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification and factual record can be powerful in demonstrating practical application or an inventive concept; eligibility often requires case-by-case analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The October 2019 update emphasizes: more guidance on 'mere instructions to apply'; practical application is broad and broader than 'inventive concept'; analyses are fact-specific and case-by-case; explicit statements in the specification about technical improvements can strengthen eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative examples (Examples 37–46) to guide analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO-provided examples (37–46) illustrate how the two-prong Step 2A and Step 2B analyses apply to different fact patterns (GUI icon relocation, audio-mixer simulation, neural-network training for facial detection, adaptive network monitoring, cryptographic communications, medical-record notifications, life-sciences diagnostics/treatment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review examples to see how specific features (e.g., particular machine/application, technical improvements, quantified thresholds) led to eligibility or ineligibility in practice (e.g., Example 40 shows two similar claims with different outcomes based on a specific traffic-monitoring threshold). Use examples to identify what made claims eligible (specific application, technical improvement) versus ineligible (generic implementation, mere instructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic drafting implications to improve eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical drafting strategies recommended to increase the likelihood that claims are found eligible under the PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include: state technical improvements explicitly in the specification; tie claims to specific technical environments; avoid pure mental-process steps; include hardware/structural elements where appropriate; quantify improvements where possible; consider adding technological problem statements. Avoid relying solely on generic computer implementation or field-of-use limitations.
